title: Keep empirical service rates separate from physical capacity bounds
applies_when: Estimating kernel headroom from a GPU specification, bandwidth microbenchmark, GEMM rate or fitted service curve.
lesson: A conditional time lower bound needs necessary work for the permitted algorithm family and an applicable upper resource capacity. Normalize vendor rates by exact SKU, per-device versus system scope, and precision/sparsity footnotes before using them. A measured rate is instead an achieved reference conditioned on shape, cache, precision, clocks and execution mode. Keep these values separate; an observation faster than the model predicts is evidence to revisit the model, not proof of exceeding hardware limits. Use resource-specific analysis to select the next experiment, then validate the production workload.
avoid_when: Do not substitute current implementation traffic for an algorithmic minimum, use nominal-clock or sparse low-precision peaks as unconditional dense bounds, transfer GB300 figures to an HGX B300 instance by architecture name alone, label cache-resident traffic as DRAM bandwidth, or treat a maximum of resource times as proof that an executable schedule attains it.

evidence.note: Official resource and Roofline analysis distinguishes hardware capacity, achieved utilization and memory hierarchy. This supports the modeling distinction, not a measured rate or optimality claim for any particular device or kernel.

NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra datasheet (October 2025), p. 5: per-GPU FP16/BF16 is 4.5 PFLOPS for HGX B300 versus 5 PFLOPS for GB300 NVL72. Footnote 2 defines these as sparse and dense as half, giving nominal dense 2.25 versus 2.5 PFLOPS. These SKU-specific ratings are not unconditional runtime bounds or achieved rates.

The HGX B300 table describes an eight-GPU system: 36 PFLOPS BF16 is sparse, with dense half that value. Divide by both the sparsity factor and GPU count for a per-device dense reference; do not assign the system figure to one visible GPU.
